In brief

Twice in the novel, Bloom thinks of "Babes in the Wood," an old ballad and nursery tale of two young children left alone in a forest. In Nausicaa he recalls it very simply and directly in connection with the fear that his young daughter experienced when her parents hid behind a tree. In Calypso he puts it to much more complex use when he imagines the servant girl next door asking a constable for help: "O please, Mr Policeman, I'm lost in the wood." This sentence joins the story of the babes with music-hall songs about country people lost in the big city and also with the name of the servant's employer, Mr. Woods. It suggests that Bloom is capable of the kind of "wit" that he admires in Molly and that readers expect of Stephen.

At more length

Originally published as a broadsheet ballad in 1595 but later included in Mother Goose nursery rhymes and in pantomimes based on them, "Babes in the Wood" tells the story of two small children left in the care of their uncle after their parents die. To steal their inheritance, he sends them off with a pair of murderers, one of whom kills the other and leaves the children to fend for themselves in the woods. They die, and birds cover their bodies with leaves.

Bloom recalls some version of the story, or song, in Nausicaa when he remembers how fearless Milly was at being tossed about on the Erin's King, but how scared she was when her parents played an impromptu game of hide-and-seek: "the women, fear of God in their faces. Milly, no sign of funk. Her blue scarf loose, laughing. Don't know what death is at that age. [...] But being lost they fear. When we hid behind the tree at Crumlin. I didn't want to. Mamma! Mamma! Babes in the wood." For him, the story speaks to children's deepseated fears of losing their parents and being unprotected from the world's dangers.

Bloom pulls up the grim story more lightly in Calypso, associating it with popular songs about policemen. In Popular Music in England, 1840-1914: A Social History (1987), Dave Russell observes that "Policemen seem to have featured in music-hall song from at least the late 1860s," often as objects of scorn (101). Some of these songs entertained audiences with stories of country bumpkins who looked to policemen for help, encouraging urbanites to enjoy themselves at the expense of naive recent arrivals. Bloom's words, "O please, Mr policeman," are those of a lyric identified by Gifford and Seidman—Oh Please, Mr. P'liceman, "written by E. Andrews and popularized in the 1890s by the Tillie Sisters." In the song a policeman laughs at some rubes:

To London Town we came, you know, a week ago today,
And 'tis the first time we've been out, and quickly lost our way;
We got somewhere near Leicester Square, when a p'liceman bold
Cried out, "Move on!" and how he laughed as we our story told.
(Chorus:) Oh, please, Mr. P'liceman, do be good to us;
We've not been long in London, and we want to take a 'bus.
They told us we could go by 'bus to Pimlico,
Oh, what wicked Place is London—Oh! Oh! Oh!

Vesta Tilley also performed a song called "Please, Sir, I've Lost My Way." It tells of a Lincolnshire villager who feels lost in the big city and is approached by a woman who says that she too has lost her way in the city and needs help. A fake policeman appears and he and the woman con the mark out of all his possessions. The man tells his woes to another policeman, at which the constable laughs and says that he has been victimized by a pair of known swindlers. And now, "I'm chaffed by all who know it, by my friends, both far and near, / And even cheeky barmaids when they serve me smile and jeer."

God knows how many variations there were on this theme, but Bloom invents his own. He imagines the servant girl telling a policeman, "I'm lost in the wood," implying that she feels threatened by her employer Mr. Woods. This man, Bloom imagines, has brought the girl into his house as "New blood" to replace his "oldish" wife, and the fact that she wears "Brown scapulars in tatters, defending her both ways," supports his fantasy. But Bloom puts a new twist on the familiar trope by supposing that this girl can take care of herself. She reports the sexual harassment to a cop in order to flirt with him: "For another: a constable off duty cuddled her in Eccles lane. They like them sizeable. Prime sausage. O please, Mr Policeman, I'm lost in the wood."

Bloom is probably imagining all of this, composing a little fictive vignette as Stephen often does. That says something about his powers of imagination. So does the fact that his mind can organize such complexity—babes lost in the feral wood, rustics lost in the big city, servant girls lost in their employers' houses—in the space of one short sentence. It shows that he can do what Molly does when she refers to Ben Dollard as "base barreltone," or Stephen when he thinks of mathematical symbols moving "in grave morrice."

John Hunt 2026
